ford.summary: A state may hear a product suit against a manufacturer that systematically served its market for the very model that injured a resident there, although the particular car was designed, built and first sold elsewhere; “arise out of or relate to” has two halves, and the second does not require causation.

sections.Parties: Ford Motor Company, incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Michigan, was the defendant in two products-liability actions and the petitioner in both. In Montana, Charles Lucero, personal representative of Markkaya Gullett’s estate, sued for Gullett and her heirs; the Montana Eighth Judicial District Court appears in the caption because Ford sought supervisory control over its refusal to dismiss. In Minnesota, Adam Bandemer, an injured passenger, sued Ford and also the driver, Eric Hanson, and Hanson’s father, who owned the car. The Supreme Court consolidated the two cases only to decide the common jurisdictional question.
sections.Material Facts: In 2015 Gullett was driving a 1996 Ford Explorer on a Montana interstate near her home when a rear tire’s tread separated; the Explorer rolled into a ditch and she died. Ford had designed it in Michigan, assembled it in Kentucky and first sold it to a Washington dealer; a decade of resales brought it to Montana. In January 2015 Bandemer rode in a 1994 Crown Victoria on a rural Minnesota road when the driver rear-ended a county snowplow; the airbag allegedly failed and he suffered a severe brain injury. That car was designed in Michigan, built in Canada and first sold in North Dakota. Ford advertised in both states by television, radio, billboards, print and direct mail, sold through 36 Montana and 84 Minnesota dealerships (Minnesota’s record showed over 2,000 model-year 1994 Crown Victorias sold in 2013–2015), and kept older cars running through dealer repairs and replacement parts.
sections.Procedural History: Ford moved to dismiss both suits for lack of personal jurisdiction and lost in each trial court. In Montana it petitioned for supervisory control; the Montana Supreme Court accepted, reviewed de novo, and upheld jurisdiction under Rule 4(b)(1)(B) and the Due Process Clause, 2019 MT 115. In Minnesota the Court of Appeals affirmed the denial, and the Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed on July 31, 2019, reading its long-arm statute to the constitutional limit; Ford had conceded the extent of its contacts and the reasonableness of litigating there and disputed only relatedness. Justice Anderson dissented with Chief Justice Gildea, and a registered-agent consent theory was left undecided. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, consolidated the cases and affirmed on March 25, 2021.
sections.Issue: May a state exercise specific jurisdiction over a manufacturer that extensively markets, sells and services the relevant vehicle model there, when that model allegedly injures a resident in a local accident but the manufacturer designed, built and first sold the particular car elsewhere? Must the plaintiff prove that the manufacturer’s forum conduct caused the claim, or can a sufficiently close relationship between that conduct and the local controversy satisfy the requirement that the claim “arise out of or relate to” the defendant’s forum contacts?
sections.Holding: Both states may hear these suits. Justice Kagan wrote for five (Roberts, Breyer, Sotomayor, Kavanaugh); Justices Alito and Gorsuch (joined by Thomas) concurred in the judgment, so all eight participating Justices agreed, Justice Barrett not taking part. Ford’s extensive advertising, sales and servicing of Explorers and Crown Victorias in each state, together with an accident there injuring a resident, sufficiently connected Ford, the forum and the litigation. The Court decided nothing about defect, causation or damages.
sections.Reasoning: Ford proposed a causation rule: only the state where it designed, built or first sold the particular car could hear the claim. Kagan gave each half of “arise out of or relate to” its own meaning: the first asks about causation, the second admits relationships without a causal showing, though “relate to” has real limits. The connection ran through the models and the market Ford systematically served: it advertised, sold, serviced and supplied parts for these very models, which then malfunctioned and injured residents on local roads. No plaintiff had to show reliance on an advertisement or a dealer; a footnote added that a recent mover would be no different. World-Wide Volkswagen’s statement that a manufacturer serving a state’s market may be sued there for a local injury was dictum, but later cases endorsed it, and fair warning plus the reciprocal benefits of the forum’s markets supported jurisdiction. Bristol-Myers differed because those nonresidents never used or were injured by the drug in California, and Walden only bars a plaintiff’s contacts from substituting for the defendant’s. Nationwide companies are not suable anywhere on any claim.

ford.separateOpinions: Justice Alito agreed that World-Wide Volkswagen answered the case but objected to parsing “arise out of or relate to” like statutory text; a commonsense, broad conception of causation (Ford’s efforts put these cars on local roads) sufficed, and a free-standing relatedness category would be hard to administer. Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Thomas, worried that replacing but-for causation with “affiliation” left courts guessing, offered a Maine duck-decoy seller as a test case, and asked why individuals face tag jurisdiction while corporations are at home in only one or two states.

cp-goodyear.summary: A foreign subsidiary is not subject to general jurisdiction in North Carolina because some of its tires reach the state through affiliated distributors; all-purpose jurisdiction requires affiliations so continuous and systematic that the corporation is essentially at home, paradigmatically its place of incorporation and principal place of business.

sections.Parties: The parents of Julian Brown and Matthew Helms, North Carolina residents, sued as administrators of their sons’ estates. The defendants were The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company, an Ohio corporation, and three indirect subsidiaries organized and operating in Luxembourg, Turkey and France. Only the three foreign subsidiaries contested personal jurisdiction and petitioned for certiorari; the American parent operated in North Carolina and did not challenge the state courts’ authority over it, and its presence did not establish jurisdiction over each separately incorporated subsidiary.
sections.Material Facts: In April 2004 the two boys, thirteen-year-old soccer players, died in a bus accident outside Paris on the way to the airport. Their parents alleged that a defective tire made at the Turkish subsidiary’s plant caused the crash and challenged its design, construction, testing and inspection. The accident, the manufacture of the tire and its sale all occurred outside North Carolina, and the tire was a type not distributed there. The subsidiaries made tires mainly for European and Asian markets, had no North Carolina place of business, employees, bank accounts or registration, and did not design, sell or ship tires there. Some of their other tires nevertheless reached the state through other Goodyear affiliates: tens of thousands out of tens of millions made, many special-order.
sections.Procedural History: The parents filed wrongful-death claims in the Superior Court for Onslow County, and the subsidiaries’ motions to dismiss were denied. The North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed, 199 N.C. App. 50 (2009): it conceded that specific jurisdiction was unavailable because the injury did not arise from North Carolina contacts, but found general jurisdiction because the subsidiaries had placed tires into an organized distribution system that carried some to North Carolina and had not taken steps to prevent it, stressing the state’s interest in a forum for its residents. The North Carolina Supreme Court denied review. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed, refusing to consider the parents’ single-enterprise theory because they had not raised it below or in opposing certiorari.
sections.Issue: Does a foreign subsidiary become subject to general personal jurisdiction in North Carolina because some tires it manufactures abroad enter the state through affiliated distribution channels, when the lawsuit concerns a different tire and a fatal accident in France? May contacts that might support specific jurisdiction over a product claim instead support adjudication of any claim against the manufacturer?
sections.Holding: No. Justice Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Court. A state may exercise general, all-purpose jurisdiction over a corporation only when its affiliations with the state are so continuous and systematic as to render it essentially at home there; the paradigm homes are the place of incorporation and the principal place of business, with Perkins illustrating a sufficiently central operation elsewhere. The subsidiaries’ limited, indirect tire distribution did not make them at home in North Carolina, so the state could not hear these unrelated claims.
sections.Reasoning: The Court began with the difference between a forum’s power over a particular dispute and its power over every dispute involving a defendant. Product distribution can create a contact relevant to a claim about that product’s presence or use in the forum; it does not create a corporate home, and treating the circulation of products as sufficient for general jurisdiction would make any substantial manufacturer answerable on any claim wherever its goods were sold. The North Carolina courts had imported stream-of-commerce reasoning into the wrong inquiry, and the plaintiffs had conceded that the forum transactions were unconnected to the accident. Their sons’ residence gave them a strong reason to want a local forum but added nothing to the subsidiaries’ own affiliations with the state. Measured against Perkins, where the president ran a Philippine company from Ohio, and Helicopteros, where substantial Texas purchases and training trips did not suffice, the subsidiaries fell far short. The parent’s operations did not erase the subsidiaries’ separate identities, and because the single-enterprise theory was forfeited the Court did not decide when affiliates’ contacts may be attributed to one another.

cp-perkins.summary: A Philippine mining company whose president ran its affairs from an Ohio office during the wartime shutdown of its mines had continuous and systematic Ohio activities substantial enough that due process permitted, though it did not compel, Ohio to hear unrelated claims against it.

sections.Parties: Idonah Slade Perkins, a nonresident of Ohio, sued as a shareholder of Benguet Consolidated Mining Company and was the petitioner in the Supreme Court. Benguet, the respondent, was a Philippine mining corporation organized as a sociedad anonima. Its president was also its general manager and principal stockholder, and his activities in Ohio were the corporate activities on which the jurisdictional question turned.
sections.Material Facts: Benguet owned gold and silver mines in the Philippines, and mining stopped during the Japanese occupation in the Second World War. The president returned to his home in Clermont County, Ohio, and ran the company from there during and immediately after the war. He kept an office and the corporate files, carried on company correspondence, drew salary checks for himself and two secretaries, maintained substantial corporate bank accounts, used an Ohio bank as stock-transfer agent, held directors’ meetings, and directed policy for rehabilitating the mines, including purchases of machinery. He was personally served in Ohio while acting there for the corporation, and the adequacy of notice was not disputed. Perkins sought about $68,400 in unpaid dividends in one action and about $2.5 million for a failure to issue 120,000 shares in another. Neither claim arose from anything done in Ohio.
sections.Procedural History: Perkins brought two actions in the Court of Common Pleas of Clermont County. Benguet challenged jurisdiction and the trial court quashed service in each; the Ohio Court of Appeals affirmed, and the Ohio Supreme Court consolidated the cases and affirmed, 155 Ohio St. 116 (1951). Its syllabus said the company could not be sued in Ohio on unrelated claims without making clear whether Ohio law or the Federal Constitution compelled that result, though Justice Taft’s opinion treated due process as forbidding jurisdiction. The United States Supreme Court, Justice Burton writing, vacated and remanded; Justice Black concurred in the result, and Justice Minton, joined by Chief Justice Vinson, dissented because he read the syllabus as an adequate state-law ground and would have dismissed the writ.
sections.Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment prevent Ohio from exercising personal jurisdiction over a Philippine corporation on claims unrelated to Ohio when the corporation’s president continuously conducts its business from an Ohio office during the suspension of its Philippine operations? If the Constitution permits jurisdiction, must Ohio exercise it?
sections.Holding: Due process permitted Ohio to entertain the unrelated claims because Benguet’s continuous and systematic corporate activities in Ohio were sufficiently substantial, but the Constitution did not compel Ohio to provide the forum; the state remained free to allow or withhold jurisdiction under its own law. The judgment was vacated so the Ohio courts could reconsider without the mistaken federal premise. Later cases treat Perkins as the example of general jurisdiction outside the paradigm homes, because Ohio functioned as the company’s temporary center of operations.
sections.Reasoning: The Court applied International Shoe’s focus on the quality and nature of corporate activity, asking whether the company’s connection with Ohio made it fair to require a defense there even for claims that arose elsewhere. Service on the president gave notice, but notice alone did not establish authority to adjudicate; both his actual role and the corporation’s business in the forum mattered. That business was extensive and central: correspondence, finances, directors’ meetings, compensation and the direction of the mines’ rehabilitation were all conducted from the Ohio office, far more than an officer’s occasional presence or a series of isolated purchases. The absence of an Ohio business license or statutory agent did not decide the constitutional question, because the company was actually carrying on business there. The Court then separated federal permission from state obligation: the Fourteenth Amendment limits state power but does not require a state to use every measure of jurisdiction the Constitution would allow. Because the Ohio judgment might have rested on a mistaken view of that limit, vacatur let Ohio decide what its own law required.

cp-helicopteros.summary: About $4 million of Texas helicopter purchases, related training trips, one negotiating visit and payments drawn on a Houston bank were not the continuous and systematic contacts needed for general jurisdiction over a Colombian carrier sued for a crash in Peru; the parties’ concession that the claims did not arise from those contacts kept specific jurisdiction out of the case.

sections.Parties: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. (Helicol), a Colombian corporation headquartered in Bogotá that provided helicopter transportation in South America, was a defendant below and the petitioner. The respondents were the survivors and representatives of four United States citizens killed in a helicopter crash in Peru; the decedents worked for a Peruvian consortium associated with Williams-Sedco-Horn, a joint venture headquartered in Houston. Bell Helicopter and the consortium entities were also defendants, but the Supreme Court’s ruling concerned jurisdiction over Helicol alone.
sections.Material Facts: On January 26, 1976 a Helicol helicopter carrying pipeline workers crashed in Peru, killing four American passengers. None of the decedents or plaintiffs was domiciled in Texas, though the workers had been hired in Houston. Helicol’s chief executive had flown to Houston in 1974 to negotiate the transportation contract (prices, fuel, housing); the contract was executed in Peru, written in Spanish and provided for disputes in Peruvian courts. Payments were drawn on a Houston bank the customer chose but received in New York and Panama City, Florida. Between 1970 and 1977 Helicol bought more than $4 million of helicopters, parts and accessories from Bell in Fort Worth, about 80 percent of its fleet, and sent pilots to Texas for training and to ferry the aircraft home; maintenance and management personnel also visited. It had no Texas office, employees, operations, bank account, real estate, license or agent for service.
sections.Procedural History: The wrongful-death suits were filed in state district court in Harris County. Helicol’s special appearances were overruled, the cases were consolidated and tried, and the jury returned a verdict against Helicol of $1,141,200. The Texas Court of Civil Appeals reversed for want of jurisdiction, 616 S.W.2d 247 (1981). The Texas Supreme Court first affirmed over three dissents, then on rehearing withdrew that opinion and reversed, again with three dissenters, treating the long-arm statute as reaching the federal limit, 638 S.W.2d 870 (1982). In the Supreme Court both sides treated the claims as neither arising out of nor related to Helicol’s Texas activities, so only general jurisdiction was presented; the Court expressly declined to decide whether “arise out of” and “relate to” describe different connections.
sections.Issue: Can Texas exercise general personal jurisdiction over a Colombian helicopter operator in wrongful-death actions arising from a crash in Peru, when the company’s Texas contacts consist of substantial purchases, related training trips, one negotiation visit and acceptance of checks drawn on a Texas bank, and the parties treat the claims as unrelated to those contacts?
sections.Holding: No. Justice Blackmun wrote for eight Justices; Justice Brennan dissented. Helicol’s contacts were not the continuous and systematic general business contacts needed to support jurisdiction over an unrelated cause of action. Purchases from a forum seller, even in substantial amounts and with accompanying training trips, do not alone authorize general jurisdiction. The Texas judgment was reversed; nothing was decided about the merits of the wrongful-death claims or the other defendants.
sections.Reasoning: The Court measured Helicol against Perkins, where the company’s business was actually managed from the forum. Helicol had no comparable office or corporate center in Texas; a single negotiating trip to Houston was nothing like continuing management from the state. The customer’s unilateral choice to pay from a Houston bank could not be attributed to Helicol as a purposeful contact. The purchases were commercially important, but under Rosenberg Bros. & Co. v. Curtis Brown Co. buying goods and sending representatives to the seller’s state does not establish the presence needed to answer unrelated suits there, and the training visits were incidental to the purchases. Helicol operated in South America and provided no services in Texas. The Court rejected a jurisdiction-by-necessity argument because the record did not show that all defendants could not be sued together in Peru or Colombia, leaving open whether such a doctrine could ever exist. Because the parties’ concession confined the case to general jurisdiction, the ruling says nothing about whether these transactions could support a related claim.

cp-helicopteros.separateOpinions: Justice Brennan dissented. He considered Helicol’s Texas dealings substantial enough for jurisdiction and, more importantly, sufficiently related to the dispute to support specific jurisdiction even if the claims did not technically arise from them: the transportation arrangement was negotiated in Houston, the helicopter had been bought in Texas and the pilot trained there. He criticized equating relatedness with strict causation, an issue the Court later took up in Ford.

cp-daimler.summary: A corporation is at home, and so subject to general jurisdiction, in its place of incorporation and principal place of business and only in an exceptional case elsewhere; even attributing Mercedes-Benz USA’s substantial California sales to Daimler, judged against the company’s worldwide operations, did not make Daimler at home in California for claims about conduct in Argentina.

sections.Parties: Twenty-two residents of Argentina sued DaimlerChrysler Aktiengesellschaft, later Daimler AG, a German company headquartered in Stuttgart; they were the respondents and Daimler the petitioner. They sought to hold Daimler responsible for the conduct of Mercedes-Benz Argentina, a subsidiary, while relying for forum contacts on a different indirect subsidiary, Mercedes-Benz USA, LLC (MBUSA), a Delaware company with its principal place of business in New Jersey. Daimler was the sole corporate defendant named in the operative complaint.
sections.Material Facts: The plaintiffs alleged that Mercedes-Benz Argentina collaborated with Argentine security forces during the 1976–1983 “Dirty War” to kidnap, detain, torture and kill workers and their relatives, and they pleaded claims under the Alien Tort Statute, the Torture Victim Protection Act and California and Argentine law. None of the conduct, victims or perpetrators had any California connection. MBUSA imported Daimler vehicles from Germany and distributed them to independent dealers; it had a regional office, a vehicle preparation center and a classic-car center in California, where its sales were about 2.4 percent of Daimler’s worldwide total. The distributor agreement called MBUSA an independent contractor buying and selling for its own account with no authority to bind Daimler. The plaintiffs nevertheless argued that MBUSA was Daimler’s agent because its distribution work was essential to Daimler’s business.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs filed in the Northern District of California in 2004. After jurisdictional discovery on the agency theory the district court dismissed, finding Daimler’s own contacts insufficient and declining to attribute MBUSA’s. A Ninth Circuit panel affirmed in 2009 with Judge Reinhardt dissenting, then on rehearing withdrew that opinion and, in an opinion by Reinhardt, 644 F.3d 909 (2011), treated MBUSA as Daimler’s agent because its services were so important that Daimler would perform them itself if MBUSA did not; rehearing en banc was denied over eight dissents. In the Supreme Court the plaintiffs did not pursue specific jurisdiction, alter ego or Daimler’s own contacts, and Daimler had not disputed that MBUSA itself was subject to general jurisdiction in California. The Court therefore assumed both that MBUSA was at home there and that its contacts could be attributed to Daimler, and reversed.
sections.Issue: May California exercise general jurisdiction over a German parent corporation for alleged misconduct in Argentina because an American subsidiary conducts substantial business in California, even assuming that the subsidiary’s contacts are attributable to the parent? Is substantial, continuous local business enough to make the parent answerable there on every claim?
sections.Holding: No. Justice Ginsburg wrote for eight Justices; Justice Sotomayor concurred in the judgment only. General jurisdiction ordinarily exists over a corporation in its state of incorporation and principal place of business, and another forum qualifies only in an exceptional case where the corporation’s operations there are so substantial and of such a nature as to render it at home. A substantial volume of business, considered in isolation, is insufficient; the assessment considers the corporation’s activities in their entirety, nationwide and worldwide. Even crediting all of MBUSA’s California contacts to Daimler, Daimler was not at home in California.
sections.Reasoning: The Ninth Circuit’s agency formulation was too broad: almost any subsidiary does work important enough that the parent would have to find another way to do it, so the test would expose a parent to general jurisdiction wherever an affiliate operated. The Court did not need to settle every attribution theory, because even the assumed attribution failed. The at-home standard gives all-purpose jurisdiction a definite scope: incorporation and principal place of business are readily ascertainable places where a company can anticipate suit on any claim, while Perkins shows that the list is not absolutely closed. California was a significant market, but so were many states and countries in which Daimler sold cars; treating every substantial market as a home would destroy predictability and restore jurisdiction over unrelated claims everywhere a large enterprise does business. The Court announced no percentage threshold; the character of the operation and its place in the whole business matter together. The international setting reinforced the point, since foreign plaintiffs sought to litigate foreign conduct through a distribution link, though the holding rested on the absence of an at-home relationship.

cp-daimler.separateOpinions: Justice Sotomayor would have assumed the contacts sufficient and held the exercise of jurisdiction unreasonable given the foreign plaintiffs, German defendant, Argentine events and an available foreign forum. She objected that the Court decided a question not developed below after Daimler had conceded the sufficiency of MBUSA’s contacts, and that comparing forum contacts with a company’s operations elsewhere lets a larger corporation escape jurisdiction that the same local activity would support against a smaller one.

cp-bnsf.summary: FELA’s venue and concurrent-jurisdiction provision confers no personal jurisdiction, and a railroad with 2,000 miles of track and 2,100 employees in Montana is not at home there; Daimler’s at-home rule applies to domestic corporations and federal claims alike, leaving only a consent theory for remand.

sections.Parties: BNSF Railway Company, incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Texas, was the defendant in two Federal Employers’ Liability Act actions and the petitioner. Robert Nelson, a North Dakota resident, was one plaintiff; Kelli Tyrrell, a South Dakota resident suing as administrator of the estate of her husband Brent Tyrrell, was the other. Both resisted dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction in Montana.
sections.Material Facts: Nelson alleged knee injuries suffered while working for BNSF as a fuel-truck driver. Tyrrell alleged that her husband developed fatal kidney cancer from exposure to carcinogenic chemicals while working for the railroad. Neither injury was connected to Montana, and neither employee appears to have worked for BNSF there. BNSF nevertheless had a substantial physical presence in the state: about 2,061 miles of track, some 2,100 employees and an automotive facility. It operated in twenty-eight states, and Montana accounted for roughly 6 percent of its track, under 5 percent of its employees and under 10 percent of its revenue. Those figures supplied the argument that BNSF was sufficiently present in Montana to be sued there on any claim.
sections.Procedural History: Nelson filed in Montana state court in March 2011 and Tyrrell in May 2014; BNSF moved to dismiss both for want of personal jurisdiction. The trial court granted the motion in Nelson’s case and denied it in Tyrrell’s. The Montana Supreme Court consolidated the appeals and let both actions proceed, 2016 MT 126, reading 45 U.S.C. § 56 to authorize jurisdiction over a railroad wherever it does business, relying on Montana Rule of Civil Procedure 4(b)(1) (persons “found within” the state), and distinguishing Daimler as a case about foreign corporations and foreign claims; Justice McKinnon dissented. The Supreme Court granted certiorari. BNSF did not contest that it was “found within” Montana under the state rule, and because the state court had not addressed the employees’ consent theory the Court left it open on remand.
sections.Issue: Does FELA authorize a state court to exercise personal jurisdiction over any railroad doing business in the state? If not, do BNSF’s extensive Montana tracks and workforce make it subject to general jurisdiction there for employment claims unconnected to Montana?
sections.Holding: No on both questions. Justice Ginsburg wrote for eight Justices; Justice Sotomayor joined the statutory analysis but dissented from the due-process holding. Section 56’s provision on where an action “may be brought” is a venue provision and its concurrent-jurisdiction clause concerns subject-matter jurisdiction; neither confers personal jurisdiction. Daimler’s at-home requirement applies to domestic railroads and FELA claims as much as to foreign corporations, and BNSF’s Montana operations did not make it at home there. The judgment was reversed and remanded, with the consent theory undecided.
sections.Reasoning: The Court separated three questions the Montana opinion had run together: subject-matter jurisdiction (authority over the type of dispute), venue (a permissible place within the system) and personal jurisdiction (authority over the particular defendant). Section 56’s language that an action may be brought in certain federal districts is the language of venue, and its statement that federal and state courts have concurrent jurisdiction ensures that state courts may hear FELA claims as a class; neither supplies authority over every railroad in every state where it lays track. When Congress means to confer broad personal jurisdiction it ordinarily speaks to service of process, which FELA does not. On due process the Court applied Goodyear and Daimler. Delaware and Texas were BNSF’s homes; Montana hosted real business but only one part of a much larger system, with no exceptional circumstance like the relocated headquarters in Perkins. The same operations could support specific jurisdiction over a claim arising from Montana activity, but these claims had no such connection, and Daimler could not be confined to multinational defendants or particular kinds of claims.

cp-bnsf.separateOpinions: Justice Sotomayor agreed that FELA confers no personal jurisdiction but renewed her objection to Daimler’s comparison of forum contacts with a company’s operations elsewhere, which she saw as favoring large multistate companies that fully enjoy a forum’s protections. Even under the at-home test she would have remanded for a fact-intensive assessment rather than rejecting exceptional-case jurisdiction herself, warning that limiting the exception to facts nearly identical to Perkins would drain it of meaning.

cp-insurance-ireland.summary: Personal jurisdiction is an individual, waivable right, so a court may treat jurisdictional facts as established under Rule 37 when a defendant that appeared to contest jurisdiction refuses, after repeated extensions and an express warning, to produce the discovery needed to decide the question; the sanction must be just and related to the withheld discovery.

sections.Parties: Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée (CBG), incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Guinea, where it mined and processed bauxite, was the plaintiff and respondent. Fourteen foreign excess insurers, including Insurance Corporation of Ireland, were the petitioners. Other insurers had been in the case: four did not contest personal jurisdiction, three won dismissal in the court of appeals, and the primary insurer, Insurance Company of North America (INA), never challenged jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts: CBG was owned 49 percent by the Republic of Guinea and 51 percent by Halco, a Pennsylvania company that handled its administration, including insurance. Halco’s broker obtained $20 million of business-interruption coverage: INA wrote the first $10 million, and twenty-one foreign insurers subscribed through the London market to the next $10 million on INA’s terms. CBG claimed that mechanical problems interrupted its operations and caused losses beyond the primary coverage; the insurers refused to pay. Because the excess insurers disputed personal jurisdiction in Pennsylvania, CBG sought records of the nature and extent of their Pennsylvania insurance business. Those records were in the insurers’ and their London brokers’ hands, and the fight over producing them became the basis of the sanction the Supreme Court reviewed.
sections.Procedural History: CBG sued in the Western District of Pennsylvania in December 1975 under diversity jurisdiction; the excess insurers raised lack of personal jurisdiction in their answer and a summary-judgment motion. CBG sought policy records from 1976 and narrowed its request to Pennsylvania policies and risks; in July 1978 the court ordered the insurers to obtain the material from their London brokers within ninety days, later extended, and the insurers offered access to some four million files in London instead. In December 1978 the judge found no conscientious effort to comply, gave sixty more days, and warned that continued default would result in a finding of personal jurisdiction under Rule 37(b)(2)(A). On April 19, 1979 he imposed that sanction. The Third Circuit affirmed solely on the sanction ground, 651 F.2d 877 (1981), and reversed as to three complying insurers. Certiorari was limited to the validity of the sanction.
sections.Issue: May a federal court treat facts supporting personal jurisdiction as established when defendants who appeared to contest jurisdiction disobey discovery orders directed to those very facts? Did the district court abuse its discretion by imposing that consequence after repeated extensions and explicit warnings?
sections.Holding: Yes, and no. Justice White wrote for eight Justices; Justice Powell concurred in the judgment. Personal jurisdiction protects an individual liberty interest and may be waived, consented to, or lost through the legal consequences of litigation conduct, so Rule 37 may establish jurisdictional facts as a sanction without violating due process. The sanction must be just and specifically related to the claim or issue the discovery order addressed; treating the withheld Pennsylvania contacts as established met that test, and the district court did not abuse its discretion. The Third Circuit was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The insurers argued that a court without personal jurisdiction cannot bind them with orders and so cannot acquire jurisdiction by punishing disobedience. The Court rejected the circularity: a defendant who appears to challenge jurisdiction submits that question for decision and must comply with the lawful procedures for resolving it, without surrendering the objection. Subject-matter jurisdiction rests on constitutional and statutory allocations of judicial power and cannot be conferred by consent or lost by inaction; personal jurisdiction is the defendant’s own due-process protection, which may be accepted by contract, waived by failure to plead, or fixed by consequences attached to the defendant’s conduct. The sanction also had an evidentiary basis: under Hammond Packing a refusal to produce relevant evidence supports a presumption that the resisting party’s position lacks merit, unlike Hovey v. Elliott, where a defense was struck to punish unrelated contempt. CBG sought evidence of Pennsylvania contacts, the insurers blocked it, and the sanction established exactly those contacts; repeated extensions, broken promises and an unmistakable warning made it just. A defendant may instead default and attack jurisdiction collaterally, but one that litigates and loses is bound.

cp-insurance-ireland.separateOpinions: Justice Powell concurred in the judgment on a narrower ground: CBG had already made a prima facie showing of minimum contacts, which justified the discovery, and the insurers’ refusal permitted the court to treat that showing as sufficient. He would not treat Rule 37 as an independent source of jurisdiction, and he warned against jurisdictional discovery on wholly speculative allegations.

cp-bremen.summary: A forum-selection clause in a negotiated international commercial contract is prima facie valid and enforced unless the resisting party clearly shows that enforcement would be unreasonable and unjust, that the clause was procured by fraud or overreaching, or that it offends a strong public policy of the forum; foreseeable inconvenience is not enough.

sections.Parties: Zapata Off-Shore Company, a Houston-based American corporation that owned the drilling rig Chaparral, was the plaintiff in the Florida admiralty action and the respondent. Unterweser Reederei, a German towing company, agreed to tow the rig with its deep-sea tug Bremen; Unterweser and the vessel were the defendants and petitioners seeking enforcement of the London forum clause. The complaint sought personal liability against Unterweser and proceeded in rem against the tug.
sections.Material Facts: In November 1967 Zapata accepted Unterweser’s bid to tow the Chaparral from Louisiana to a site off Ravenna, Italy. Zapata reviewed the contract and made several changes but left untouched a clause requiring any dispute to be treated before the London Court of Justice and two provisions relieving Unterweser of responsibility for certain damage to the rig. The Bremen left Louisiana on January 5, 1968. Four days later a storm in international waters in the Gulf of Mexico broke off the rig’s raised legs and seriously damaged it, and at Zapata’s direction the tug took the rig to Tampa, the nearest port of refuge. That emergency landing supplied the only American connection; the parties had contemplated a voyage through many jurisdictions and chosen London as a neutral, experienced maritime forum before any accident.
sections.Procedural History: On January 12, 1968 Zapata sued in admiralty in Tampa for $3.5 million for negligent towage and breach of contract; the tug was arrested and released on security. Unterweser moved to dismiss or stay, and in February sued Zapata in the English High Court, which enforced the clause over Zapata’s special appearance. With the six-month deadline for limiting maritime liability approaching and its motion undecided, Unterweser filed a limitation action in Tampa on July 2, 1968. The district court then denied the motion, applying forum non conveniens balancing under circuit precedent hostile to forum clauses and putting the burden on Unterweser, and in January 1969 enjoined the English action. A divided Fifth Circuit panel affirmed, and the en banc court adopted the panel opinion with six of fourteen judges dissenting, 428 F.2d 888 and 446 F.2d 907. The Supreme Court granted certiorari.
sections.Issue: Should a federal admiralty court enforce a freely negotiated international agreement requiring litigation in London, or may it disregard the clause because the American forum is convenient and foreign law might enforce liability limitations disfavored at home? Did Unterweser surrender the clause by filing a protective limitation action in the United States?
sections.Holding: Chief Justice Burger wrote for the Court; Justice White concurred and Justice Douglas dissented. The clause was prima facie valid and should be enforced unless Zapata clearly showed that enforcement would be unreasonable and unjust, that the clause resulted from fraud or overreaching, or that enforcement would contravene a strong public policy of the forum. Foreseeable inconvenience is insufficient; the resisting party must show that trial in the chosen forum would be so gravely difficult that it would for all practical purposes be deprived of its day in court. Unterweser’s limitation filing was not a waiver. The judgment was vacated and remanded for reconsideration under that standard.
sections.Reasoning: The Court discarded the idea that enforcing a forum clause improperly ousts a court of jurisdiction: the agreement did not remove the American court’s power but determined whether it should exercise that power beyond giving effect to the agreed forum. Two sophisticated businesses from different countries had arranged a costly international tow along a route where an accident could occur anywhere; an agreed neutral forum with maritime expertise reduced that uncertainty and was part of the allocation of risk and price. The lower courts had put the burden on the wrong party: a plaintiff that had promised to litigate in London could not escape by showing that Tampa was now preferable, and findings about Gulf Coast witnesses did not show deprivation of a meaningful opportunity to litigate. The prospect that English law would enforce the exculpatory clauses did not establish a controlling public-policy objection, since Bisso’s concern with towage in American waters did not govern a negotiated international undertaking. The limitation action was defensive, filed only because a statutory deadline was about to run, and treating it as abandonment would let Zapata’s own breach cost Unterweser its rights.

cp-bremen.separateOpinions: Justice White joined except for comments on matters left for remand, which he preferred the district court address first. Justice Douglas dissented: by invoking the limitation court Unterweser submitted to its full equitable authority, including the injunction against the English action, and the forum clause served to obtain enforcement of exculpatory terms contrary to American maritime policy, while Tampa offered practical advantages.

carnival.summary: A reasonable forum-selection clause in a non-negotiated cruise ticket is not invalid merely because it was not bargained for; it remains subject to review for fundamental fairness, fraud, overreaching and grave inconvenience, and the Shutes, having conceded notice, did not carry the heavy burden needed to avoid the Florida clause.

sections.Parties: Eulala and Russel Shute, a married couple from Washington, were the plaintiffs and respondents; Mrs. Shute alleged injury from the negligence of the cruise line and its employees, and both spouses wanted to litigate in Washington. Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc., with its principal place of business in Florida, was the defendant and petitioner seeking enforcement of the ticket’s Florida forum clause.
sections.Material Facts: The Shutes bought passage on a seven-day cruise aboard the Tropicale through a travel agent in Arlington, Washington. Their payment went to Carnival’s Miami headquarters, which then issued the tickets. A notice on the ticket’s face directed passengers to the contract conditions on its final pages; one provision made acceptance of the ticket acceptance of its terms, and another required all disputes connected with the contract to be litigated exclusively in a court in Florida. The Shutes boarded in Los Angeles and sailed to Puerto Vallarta, Mexico; in international waters off Mexico Mrs. Shute slipped on a deck mat while touring the galley. The clause was a standardized term the Shutes had no practical power to negotiate, and the ticket also restricted refunds. The Shutes essentially conceded notice before the Supreme Court, which expressly limited its decision in light of that concession.
sections.Procedural History: The Shutes sued in admiralty in the Western District of Washington. Carnival moved for summary judgment on two grounds, the Florida clause and lack of personal jurisdiction, and the district court granted the motion on the constitutional ground without finding that Florida litigation was impossible for the Shutes. The Ninth Circuit first reversed in 1988, then withdrew that opinion to certify the long-arm question to the Washington Supreme Court, which answered that the claim arose from Carnival’s Washington advertising. The Ninth Circuit reissued its opinion, 897 F.2d 377 (1990), finding jurisdiction under a but-for theory linking solicitation, purchase and injury, and refusing to enforce the clause because it was not bargained for and because the Shutes could not afford to sue in Florida. The Supreme Court reversed on the forum-clause ground alone and did not decide the personal-jurisdiction question.
sections.Issue: Is a reasonable forum-selection clause in a standard passenger ticket unenforceable merely because the passengers did not negotiate it? Did the asserted inconvenience of Florida, or the federal statute protecting injured passengers, require that the clause be set aside?
sections.Holding: Justice Blackmun wrote for seven Justices; Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Marshall, dissented. A non-negotiated forum clause in a form passage contract is not invalid for lack of bargaining, though it remains subject to judicial scrutiny for fundamental fairness, fraud, overreaching and grave inconvenience. The Shutes did not carry The Bremen’s heavy burden. The clause also did not violate the passenger-protection statute then at 46 U.S.C. App. § 183c, because it preserved adjudication by a competent court and did not limit Carnival’s liability. The Ninth Circuit was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: The Court read The Bremen’s emphasis on free negotiation in context. Bargaining is realistic between corporations arranging an international tow and unrealistic for a passenger buying a cruise ticket, but that difference does not make a reasonable clause categorically unenforceable; it calls for scrutiny that fits standardized passenger contracts. Carnival had a legitimate interest in limiting the forums in which it could be sued, since its passengers come from everywhere; a clause fixed in advance dispels confusion about where to sue, spares litigation over forum and, the majority reasoned, produces savings likely reflected in lower fares. Florida was Carnival’s principal place of business and the port for many of its cruises, so it was not chosen to discourage claims, and with notice conceded the majority presumed the Shutes could have rejected the contract. The inconvenience showing failed because the district court had made no finding of physical or financial inability. The statute forbade ticket terms relieving a carrier of negligence liability or weakening the right to trial in a competent court; selecting among competent courts did neither.

carnival.separateOpinions: Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Marshall, dissented. Passengers receive the conditions only after paying, a separate nonrefund provision made rejection costly, and fine print and unequal bargaining power undermined meaningful assent. He read the passenger-protection statute to reach a distant forum that weakens the practical right to recover even without eliminating liability, and he thought a negotiated commercial clause like The Bremen’s did not settle a consumer ticket. The ticket facsimiles in the supplement accompany his dissent.

cp-zippo.summary: An out-of-state internet business that knowingly contracts with about 3,000 forum subscribers and seven local access providers and transmits the allegedly infringing material to them sits at the commercial end of a passive-to-active spectrum and is subject to specific jurisdiction where those subscribers are; merely posting information accessible from the forum would not suffice.

sections.Parties: Zippo Manufacturing Company, a Pennsylvania corporation headquartered in Bradford that makes Zippo lighters and owned the trademarks, was the plaintiff. Zippo Dot Com, Inc., a California corporation headquartered in Sunnyvale that ran an internet news service, was the defendant moving to dismiss or transfer. The shared name reflected the trademark dispute; the businesses were unrelated. District Judge Sean J. McLaughlin of the Western District of Pennsylvania decided the motion on January 16, 1997.
sections.Material Facts: Dot Com used the domains zippo.com, zippo.net and zipponews.com. Its site offered information, advertising and an application for its news service; paid subscribers received passwords and could read and download newsgroup messages stored on California servers, paying by credit card over the internet or by telephone after supplying their names and addresses. Of about 140,000 paying subscribers worldwide, roughly 3,000, about 2 percent, lived in Pennsylvania, and Dot Com had contracts with seven Pennsylvania internet access providers, two in the Western District, to let their customers use the service. It had no Pennsylvania offices, employees or agents. Manufacturing alleged trademark infringement, dilution and false designation from the use of “Zippo” in the domains, website and message headings; messages downloaded into Pennsylvania carried the designation, and some contained sexually explicit material relevant to dilution.
sections.Procedural History: Manufacturing filed a five-count complaint asserting federal trademark claims, Pennsylvania dilution, an accounting and a constructive trust. Dot Com moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(2) and improper venue under Rule 12(b)(3), or to transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1406(a). Once jurisdiction was challenged Manufacturing bore the burden of a prima facie showing; it relied on specific jurisdiction only and conceded it was not asserting general jurisdiction. Pennsylvania’s long-arm statute reached a defendant contracting to supply services in the state and extended to the constitutional limit. The court denied the motion in full. It is a district-court ruling on a pretrial motion, not a decision on infringement or damages.
sections.Issue: Does an out-of-state internet service provider purposefully establish contacts supporting specific jurisdiction when it knowingly contracts with thousands of forum residents and local access providers and transmits material bearing the allegedly infringing mark into the forum? Is venue proper in the plaintiff’s chosen district under the federal venue statute as it stood in 1997?
sections.Holding: Yes on both questions. The court described a spectrum keyed to the nature and quality of commercial activity conducted online: knowing, repeated transmission of files under contracts with forum residents supports jurisdiction; merely posting information accessible from the forum does not; intermediate interactive sites are judged by the degree of interaction and the commercial character of the exchanges. Dot Com’s subscriptions and continuing deliveries put it at the commercial end, those contacts gave rise to the infringement claims, and jurisdiction was reasonable. Venue was proper under §§ 1391(b)(1) and (c) because the corporate defendant resided wherever it was subject to personal jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning: The court treated internet transactions as a way of doing ordinary interstate business. Dot Com did more than advertise a website: it processed Pennsylvania customers’ applications, took their money, issued passwords and repeatedly transmitted the service they had bought, knowing their addresses. Dot Com argued that Pennsylvanians had initiated contact by finding the site, so the business was fortuitous; the court answered that Dot Com controlled whether to accept each subscription and continue delivering. The 2 percent share of subscribers was no exemption, since specific jurisdiction turns on the quality and nature of the forum relationships rather than their share of worldwide business, and 3,000 continuing contracts plus seven provider agreements were substantial purposeful activity for a dispute arising from them. Relatedness came from the messages themselves, which carried the disputed designation into Pennsylvania where subscribers viewed them, injuring a Pennsylvania mark owner. Pennsylvania’s interest in protecting a resident’s marks outweighed the burden on a California business of answering for transactions it had deliberately undertaken. The sliding scale is a district court’s description of these facts, not a Supreme Court rule.

cp-shaffer.summary: Every assertion of state-court jurisdiction, including in rem and quasi in rem, must satisfy International Shoe; Delaware could not adjudicate unrelated claims against nonresident Greyhound officers and directors by sequestering stock that a statute deemed located in Delaware, because property unrelated to the claim is not by itself a sufficient contact.

sections.Parties: Arnold Heitner, a nonresident of Delaware who owned one share of Greyhound Corporation stock, brought a shareholder derivative action, suing on a claim belonging to the corporation. He named Greyhound (incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in Phoenix), its subsidiary Greyhound Lines (incorporated in California, also in Phoenix) and twenty-eight present or former officers and directors, none a Delaware resident. The twenty-one individuals whose property was sequestered challenged jurisdiction and were the appellants.
sections.Material Facts: Heitner alleged that the officers and directors had breached their duties by causing Greyhound and its subsidiary to engage in conduct in Oregon that produced a private antitrust judgment of more than $13 million and $600,000 in criminal contempt fines. The suit did not dispute ownership of their stock. Delaware’s sequestration statute let a court seize a nonresident defendant’s in-state property to compel a personal appearance, and a companion statute deemed shares of a Delaware corporation to be located in Delaware wherever the owner or the certificates were. Heitner used those provisions to sequester the individuals’ shares, options and related interests; the sequestrator placed stop-transfer orders covering about 82,000 shares of nineteen defendants and options of two more, none of the certificates being in Delaware. The property would be released on a general appearance, so a defendant could not defend the merits while limiting exposure to the seized assets.
sections.Procedural History: Heitner filed in the Delaware Court of Chancery for New Castle County on May 22, 1974 and obtained the sequestration order the same day; the defendants received notice by certified mail and publication. Twenty-one individuals appeared specially, moved to quash service and vacate the sequestration, arguing that the ex parte seizure lacked safeguards, that the property was not attachable in Delaware and that they lacked minimum contacts. The Court of Chancery rejected the challenges, treating sequestration as a means of compelling appearance, and the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed, 361 A.2d 225 (1976), holding International Shoe inapplicable because jurisdiction rested on property in the state rather than on the defendants’ contacts. The Supreme Court noted probable jurisdiction on appeal before any trial, treated the state judgment as final under Cox Broadcasting, and reversed without reaching the separate challenge to the seizure procedure.
sections.Issue: May a state obtain jurisdiction over nonresident individuals on an unrelated claim solely by declaring their stock to be located in the state and seizing it? Must the standards of International Shoe apply to in rem and quasi in rem jurisdiction, and did the defendants’ stock ownership or corporate positions supply adequate contacts?
sections.Holding: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices Stewart, White, Blackmun and Powell; Justice Brennan joined Parts I–III but dissented from the application; Justice Powell also concurred, Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment, and Justice Rehnquist did not participate. All assertions of state-court jurisdiction must be evaluated under International Shoe, because a proceeding against property ultimately adjudicates persons’ interests in it. Property may supply relevant contacts, especially when the suit concerns rights in the property itself, but the statutory presence of unrelated stock and the defendants’ corporate positions did not sustain Delaware’s jurisdiction. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Under Pennoyer, power over property in the state sufficed to adjudicate interests in it even against an owner who could not otherwise be sued there. International Shoe shifted the inquiry to the relationship among the defendant, the forum and the litigation, and there was no reason to apply that fairness inquiry to a direct personal claim while letting the identical claim escape scrutiny because the plaintiff attached an asset; in rem and quasi in rem proceedings both affect people. Where ownership or possession of land is the dispute, local property usually supplies strong contacts, so many traditional property cases still pass. Here the Greyhound stock was leverage, not the subject of the derivative claim; the alleged wrong was misconduct in Oregon, and Delaware’s statutory situs for intangible shares could not supply the missing relationship by legislative declaration. Attachment could still secure a judgment sought where jurisdiction exists (footnote 36), and the Court reserved the case where no other forum is available (footnote 37). Delaware’s interest in supervising fiduciaries did not help: applying Delaware corporate law was a choice-of-law question, not a source of adjudicatory authority.

cp-shaffer.separateOpinions: Justice Powell would have reserved whether property with a fixed, unmistakable location, particularly real estate, could alone support jurisdiction up to its value. Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment because an ordinary securities purchaser lacked fair warning of being forced into unrelated Delaware litigation. Justice Brennan agreed that International Shoe governs property-based jurisdiction but objected to deciding the contacts question on a record developed under a framework where contacts did not matter; he also thought acceptance of fiduciary duties under Delaware law ordinarily supplies a substantial relationship.

cp-burnham.summary: Personal service on an individual voluntarily present in the forum supports jurisdiction over an unrelated claim: all nine Justices agreed, but Scalia’s plurality rested on the rule’s unbroken historical pedigree while Brennan’s four Justices required and found contemporary fairness.

sections.Parties: Dennis Burnham, a New Jersey resident, was the husband and defendant in a California divorce proceeding; he petitioned for relief from the California court’s assertion of jurisdiction and then sought Supreme Court review. Francie Burnham, his estranged wife, had moved to California with their children and filed the action there. The Superior Court appears in the caption because Dennis sought extraordinary relief against the trial court’s ruling rather than appealing a final decree.
sections.Material Facts: The Burnhams married in West Virginia in 1976 and moved to New Jersey in 1977, where their two children were born. In July 1987 they agreed to separate: Francie would move to California with the children and file for divorce on grounds of irreconcilable differences. In October Dennis instead filed a New Jersey divorce complaint alleging desertion, without having a summons issued or serving Francie. She filed in California in early January 1988. Later that month Dennis traveled to southern California on business and then to the Bay Area to see his children; he took the older child to San Francisco for the weekend, and on January 24, when he returned the child to Francie’s home, he was personally served with the California summons and petition. His presence was voluntary and knowing, his visits were brief, and nothing about the divorce arose from his California activities.
sections.Procedural History: Dennis made a special appearance and moved to quash service for lack of personal jurisdiction, arguing that a few short trips for business and to see his children were insufficient contacts for the divorce action. The Superior Court denied the motion. He sought mandamus in the California Court of Appeal for the First Appellate District, which denied relief on the ground that personal service on a defendant physically present in the state is a valid basis for jurisdiction. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review that judgment and affirmed. It decided nothing about marital status, property, support or custody, or about the effect of the unserved New Jersey complaint.
sections.Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment permit a state court to exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident individual personally served while voluntarily and temporarily in the state, when the lawsuit does not arise from the activities that brought him there? After International Shoe and Shaffer, must the plaintiff separately establish claim-related minimum contacts despite valid in-state personal service?
sections.Holding: Yes, jurisdiction was proper, and no, no further showing was required on these facts. Justice Scalia announced the judgment, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Kennedy and, for most parts, Justice White; Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Marshall, Blackmun and O’Connor, concurred in the judgment; Justices White and Stevens each wrote separately. All nine agreed that personal service on Dennis while he was voluntarily in California supported jurisdiction, but no single rationale for transient (“tag”) jurisdiction commanded five votes. The California Court of Appeal was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Scalia began with the long acceptance, in English and American courts around the adoption of the Fourteenth Amendment and continuously since, of jurisdiction over individuals served within the state; an established and still-followed method helps define the traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice that International Shoe invoked. International Shoe expanded jurisdiction over absent defendants by supplying a way to judge their relationship to a state when service within it was unavailable; it did not make actual presence insufficient. Shaffer concerned absent individuals whose unrelated property a statute assigned to the forum, and its broad language did not compel identical treatment of someone personally present; this part had only three votes. Brennan read International Shoe and Shaffer to require every jurisdictional rule, old or new, to satisfy contemporary due process; history mattered because it gave fair warning, not because it was conclusive. A voluntary visitor uses the state’s roads and police, participates in its economy and may invoke its courts, so exempting him from suit would create an asymmetry. Because Dennis was knowingly and voluntarily in California, jurisdiction was fair.

cp-burnham.separateOpinions: Justice White agreed that personal service sufficed and would not upset a traditional rule absent a showing that it was so arbitrary in its general operation as to violate due process, at least where the defendant’s presence is intentional; he did not join Scalia’s full treatment of Shaffer. Justice Stevens found the historical evidence, continuing consensus, fairness and common sense together sufficient and saw no need to resolve the broader dispute; his was the ninth vote for the judgment, leaving neither rationale an opinion of the Court.

cp-mallory.summary: Enforcing Pennsylvania’s express rule that a foreign corporation’s registration to do business is consent to general jurisdiction does not violate due process, because Pennsylvania Fire (1917) controls and was never overruled; five Justices agreed on that narrow ground, the broader consent theory drew only four, and a dormant Commerce Clause challenge remained open on remand.

sections.Parties: Robert Mallory, a former Norfolk Southern freight-car mechanic who lived in Virginia when he sued, was the plaintiff and petitioner. Norfolk Southern Railway Company, then incorporated and headquartered in Virginia, was the defendant and respondent. The question was whether Pennsylvania could hear Mallory’s unrelated FELA claim on the strength of the railroad’s Pennsylvania registration rather than any contacts between the claim and the state.
sections.Material Facts: Mallory worked for the railroad for almost twenty years in Ohio and Virginia, spraying asbestos on boxcar pipes, handling chemicals in a paint shop and demolishing car interiors containing carcinogens. After leaving the railroad he lived for a time in Pennsylvania, then returned to Virginia; he was diagnosed with cancer and attributed it to his work. He alleged no exposure in Pennsylvania. Norfolk Southern nonetheless did substantial business there: more than 2,000 miles of track, eleven rail yards and three locomotive repair shops. It had registered to do business in Pennsylvania in 1998, kept the registration current, and designated a commercial registered office provider for service. Pennsylvania’s statutes made qualification as a foreign corporation a sufficient basis for general jurisdiction over any cause of action. Mallory relied on that legal act as consent rather than trying to show that the railroad was at home in Pennsylvania.
sections.Procedural History: Mallory filed his FELA action in the Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas in September 2017. The court sustained Norfolk Southern’s preliminary objections and dismissed with prejudice on February 7, 2018, reasoning that the scheme forced corporations to choose between doing business in Pennsylvania and surrendering their jurisdictional protection. While his appeal was pending in the Superior Court, that court decided Webb-Benjamin, treating registration as consent; in October 2020 the appeal was transferred to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, which has exclusive jurisdiction over orders holding a state statute unconstitutional. On December 22, 2021 it affirmed, 266 A.3d 542, holding that registration compelled as a condition of doing business was not voluntary consent and that International Shoe had displaced Pennsylvania Fire. The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari on the due-process question only and vacated and remanded on June 27, 2023; the railroad’s dormant Commerce Clause objection, undecided below, remained open.
sections.Issue: Does the Due Process Clause forbid Pennsylvania from requiring an out-of-state corporation to submit to general personal jurisdiction as a condition of registering to do business, when the company knowingly complied with that express scheme and is sued on a claim unrelated to Pennsylvania? Did International Shoe and the at-home cases displace Pennsylvania Fire Insurance Co. v. Gold Issue Mining & Milling Co., 243 U.S. 93 (1917)?
sections.Holding: No. Justice Gorsuch announced the judgment; Parts I and III-B of his opinion (Gorsuch, Thomas, Alito, Sotomayor, Jackson) are the opinion of the Court, while Parts II, III-A and IV are a four-Justice plurality without Alito. On Pennsylvania’s scheme and these facts, enforcing registration-based consent did not violate due process: Pennsylvania Fire controlled a materially identical situation and had not been overruled, and lower courts must follow directly controlling precedent even when they perceive tension with a later line. The Court did not decide whether every state’s registration statute creates consent or whether the scheme violates the dormant Commerce Clause. Justice Jackson concurred; Justice Alito concurred in part and in the judgment; Justice Barrett dissented with Roberts, Kagan and Kavanaugh.
sections.Reasoning: The five-Justice portion relied on the close fit with Pennsylvania Fire, where an Arizona plaintiff sued a Pennsylvania insurer in Missouri over Colorado property because the insurer had complied with a Missouri law requiring an appointment for service understood to cover any suit. Norfolk Southern had likewise registered under an explicit law attaching all-purpose jurisdiction and kept that status while doing substantial local business; that Mallory lived in Virginia and his exposures occurred elsewhere made no difference, since the 1917 case also involved an out-of-state plaintiff and claim. The plurality went further: registration-based consent resembles personal service on a visiting individual, states have long required foreign corporations to accept local adjudicatory authority as the price of entering their markets, International Shoe added a route to jurisdiction over nonconsenting corporations without abolishing consent, and Burnham shows that minimum contacts did not displace every traditional basis. A defendant may waive an individual due-process protection through conduct with known legal consequences. Alito declined to join that broader reasoning, so separate the majority holding from the plurality’s theory.

cp-mallory.separateOpinions: Justice Jackson framed the result as waiver under Insurance Corp. of Ireland: personal jurisdiction is an individual, waivable right, and the railroad chose registration and the benefits of local business knowing the consequence. Justice Alito supplied the fifth vote under Pennsylvania Fire but suggested a substantial prospect that compelling out-of-state businesses to defend unrelated claims burdens interstate commerce, a question left for remand. Justice Barrett, with Roberts, Kagan and Kavanaugh, dissented: labeling compelled registration “consent” lets a legislature evade Goodyear, Daimler and BNSF, the registration paperwork itself promised no jurisdiction, and Burnham’s tradition has no counterpart in unlimited registration jurisdiction.

cp-asahi.summary: Eight Justices held that California could not fairly adjudicate a Taiwanese tube maker’s indemnity claim against a Japanese valve maker after the injured Californian’s claims had settled; on minimum contacts the Court split four (O’Connor: awareness plus conduct purposefully directed at the forum) to four (Brennan: awareness of a regular and anticipated flow suffices), with Stevens declining to decide.

sections.Parties: Asahi Metal Industry Co., Ltd., a Japanese corporation that made tire-tube valve assemblies in Japan, was the petitioner and cross-defendant. Cheng Shin Rubber Industrial Co., Ltd., a Taiwanese tube manufacturer that incorporated Asahi’s valves into finished tubes, was the real party in interest seeking indemnification from Asahi. The Superior Court of Solano County was the nominal respondent because Asahi sought a writ against its ruling. The original plaintiff, Gary Zurcher, was the injured motorcyclist; his wife and passenger, Ruth Ann Moreno, died. Their claims settled before the Supreme Court decided the jurisdictional dispute.
sections.Material Facts: On September 23, 1978 Zurcher’s motorcycle crashed on Interstate 80 in Solano County, California; he blamed a defective tire, tube and sealant. Asahi sold its valve assemblies to Cheng Shin in Taiwan, shipping them from Japan: 150,000 in 1978, 500,000 in each of 1979 and 1980, and 100,000 in each of 1981 and 1982, sales that were 1.24 percent of Asahi’s income in 1981 and 0.44 percent in 1982. Cheng Shin sold tubes worldwide and said about 20 percent of its United States sales were in California. Its manager declared that Asahi knew its valves would reach California; Asahi’s president declared that the company never contemplated California litigation. A 1983 survey of one Solano County motorcycle shop found about 115 tubes, 21 bearing Asahi’s circled-A mark and 12 of those in Cheng Shin tubes. Asahi had no California office, agents, property or sales and did not control Cheng Shin’s distribution.
sections.Procedural History: Zurcher sued in the Solano County Superior Court in September 1979; Cheng Shin cross-complained against Asahi for indemnity. California’s long-arm statute, Code of Civil Procedure § 410.10, reaches the constitutional limit, and Cheng Shin bore the burden of proving jurisdiction by declarations. On April 20, 1983 the trial court denied Asahi’s motion to quash, reasoning that a business operating internationally could defend an international product claim. The Court of Appeal issued a peremptory writ directing that service be quashed. The California Supreme Court reversed and discharged the writ, 39 Cal. 3d 35 (1985): Chief Justice Bird’s majority found that Asahi intentionally placed components in a regular distribution stream knowing they would reach California; Justice Lucas, joined by Justice Mosk, dissented. By then Zurcher’s claims had settled, leaving only the indemnity dispute. The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari, 475 U.S. 1044 (1986), and unanimously reversed on February 24, 1987.
sections.Issue: Does a foreign component manufacturer establish minimum contacts with California by regularly selling components to a foreign finished-product manufacturer while aware that some finished products will be sold in California? And once the California plaintiff’s claims have settled, does the exercise of jurisdiction over the remaining indemnity dispute between a Taiwanese buyer and a Japanese seller over sales made in Asia comport with fair play and substantial justice?
sections.Holding: Jurisdiction failed. Justice O’Connor’s Part I was unanimous, and eight Justices (all but Scalia) joined Part II-B, the holding of the Court: the international burden on Asahi, California’s slight remaining interest after settlement, Cheng Shin’s failure to show that California was more convenient than Taiwan or Japan, and the interests of foreign sovereigns made jurisdiction unreasonable. On minimum contacts no view had five votes. Parts II-A and III (O’Connor, Rehnquist, Powell, Scalia) required conduct purposefully directed at the forum beyond awareness; Brennan (White, Marshall, Blackmun) found contacts from awareness of a regular and anticipated flow; Stevens (White, Blackmun) found it unnecessary to decide and suggested that volume, value and hazardous character bear on purposeful availment.
sections.Reasoning: World-Wide Volkswagen supplied the framework: a forum connection created by the defendant’s own purposeful conduct, then five fairness considerations (the defendant’s burden, the forum’s interest, the plaintiff’s interest in relief, systemic efficiency and the shared policies of the sovereigns concerned). On the controlling fairness question, defending in California would force a Japanese company across a great distance into a foreign legal system; Cheng Shin, a Taiwanese corporation seeking indemnity for sales made in Taiwan, offered no reason why California was better than Taiwan or Japan; California’s interest in a foreign indemnity dispute was slight once the tort case had settled; and in an international case the several-states factor expands to include other nations’ policies and federal foreign-relations interests. O’Connor’s plurality treated placement in the stream of commerce as commercial participation and demanded additional forum-directed acts, such as designing for the forum, advertising there, maintaining channels for advice to forum customers, or marketing through a distributor that agreed to serve the forum; Asahi had none. Brennan answered that a participant who knows the final product is regularly marketed in the forum profits from those sales and the forum’s laws, so awareness suffices.

cp-asahi.separateOpinions: Justice Brennan, with White, Marshall and Blackmun, concurred in Part II-B and the judgment but found minimum contacts from Asahi’s knowledge of a regular and anticipated flow into California. Justice Stevens, with White and Blackmun, would have rested solely on fairness, questioned describing Asahi’s hundreds of thousands of annual deliveries as bare placement, and identified volume, value and hazardous character as relevant to any contacts inquiry. Justice Scalia joined the O’Connor plurality and the judgment but not Part II-B.

cp-nicastro.summary: New Jersey lacked jurisdiction over a British machine maker on a record showing one confirmed New Jersey sale through an independent national distributor and no New Jersey-directed conduct; Kennedy’s four-Justice plurality demanded submission to the forum sovereign, while Breyer and Alito concurred only because an isolated sale failed under existing precedent.

sections.Parties: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. (McIntyre UK), an English corporation that designed and manufactured metal-recycling machinery, was the defendant and petitioner. Robert Nicastro, a New Jersey worker injured by a McIntyre Model 640 Shear, sued individually and as administrator of the estate of Roseanne Nicastro. McIntyre Machinery America, Ltd., the independent exclusive United States distributor based in Ohio, and Curcio Scrap Metal, Nicastro’s employer and the machine’s purchaser, were separately owned participants below.
sections.Material Facts: On October 11, 2001 a three-ton Model 640 Shear severed four fingers from Nicastro’s right hand at Curcio Scrap Metal in Saddle Brook, New Jersey; he alleged that the shear lacked a safety guard. Curcio had seen the machine at a Las Vegas scrap-recycling convention in 1994 or 1995 and bought it from McIntyre America in 1995 for $24,900, shipped from Ohio. McIntyre UK had appointed McIntyre America its exclusive distributor for the whole United States; its officials attended annual industry conventions with the distributor in Chicago, Las Vegas, New Orleans, Orlando, San Diego and San Francisco, never in New Jersey. Its materials referred to United States safety standards. Discovery showed at most four machines in New Jersey and only the accident machine as a confirmed sale there, no New Jersey office, property, advertising or employees, and no regular flow of machines into the state.
sections.Procedural History: Nicastro sued in the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Bergen County, in September 2003 for defective design and inadequate warnings. The trial court dismissed for want of jurisdiction; the Appellate Division reversed and ordered jurisdictional discovery; the trial court dismissed again. The Appellate Division reversed a second time, 399 N.J. Super. 539 (2008), finding O’Connor’s stream-of-commerce-plus test met by the national distributorship, trade-show activity and design for United States standards. The New Jersey Supreme Court affirmed, 201 N.J. 48 (2010), holding a foreign manufacturer amenable when it knew or should have known that a nationwide distribution system might produce sales in any state and took no reasonable step to exclude New Jersey. The United States Supreme Court reversed 6–3 on June 27, 2011: Kennedy wrote for four (Roberts, Scalia, Thomas); Breyer, joined by Alito, concurred in the judgment; Ginsburg, joined by Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented.
sections.Issue: May New Jersey exercise specific personal jurisdiction over a British manufacturer in a products-liability action arising from a machine sold and causing injury in New Jersey, when the manufacturer cultivated the United States market through an independent national distributor and trade shows, the record shows one confirmed New Jersey sale, and no conduct was directed specifically at New Jersey?
sections.Holding: No, on this record. Justice Breyer’s concurrence, the narrowest ground supporting the judgment, held that one isolated sale, national marketing outside New Jersey and no regular flow of machines or New Jersey-specific effort failed to establish purposeful availment under World-Wide Volkswagen and the Asahi opinions; Nicastro bore the burden and proved a single sale. The plurality would require conduct showing an intent to invoke or benefit from New Jersey’s sovereign authority.
